tweets.text:
AI and software stocks are now rising together.

The 1-month correlation between AI-related stocks and software stocks has risen +0.70 over the last month, to +0.15, marking its largest monthly increase since July 2025.

By comparison, the 1-month correlation was as low as -0.56 in July 2026, as investors increasingly viewed AI as a threat to traditional software businesses.

As a result, hedge fund exposure to software and services stocks declined -5 percentage points over the 12 months ending July, to just ~1% of total global hedge fund market exposure, near its lowest level on record.

The recent increase in correlation comes as some software firms previously viewed as vulnerable to AI are actually finding ways to use the technology to strengthen their existing businesses, improve productivity, and defend their competitive advantages.

Meanwhile, the US software ETF, $IGV, is up +39% since its April low, recovering most of its drawdown that began in October 2025.

The AI trade may be shifting from disruption to adaptation.

tweets.text:
🇺🇸 The share of corporate output going to workers fell to 52.8% in the second quarter, the lowest level since the series began in 1947 ⚠. That number partly explains why US corporate profits remain so strong.

➡️ The labor share is the share of output that goes to workers through compensation. A decline mainly means that compensation is growing more slowly than the value companies are creating. So a company can pay its employees more in absolute terms while still seeing labor capture a smaller share of the economic pie. Obviously, that leaves mechanically more room for margins, profits and returns to capital, and that is why the current setup is so favorable for equities.

📈 US companies are still generating productivity gains while unit labor costs remain relatively contained. They are producing more without their wage bill rising at the same pace which directly supports margins and earnings. It also explains why a cooling labor market is not necessarily inconsistent with a resilient stock market. If each worker generates more output, profits can keep growing without strong employment growth.

📉 The decline in labor’s share has been unfolding for decades, driven by globalization, automation, weaker worker bargaining power, corporate concentration and the growing importance of intangible assets. However, AI could become a powerful accelerator of that trend and this is what we are probably witnessing.

⚠️ In the short term, this is clearly very supportive for markets but over the long term, there is an obvious limit. An economy that relies heavily on household consumption cannot indefinitely increase the share of income going to capital if labor incomes fail to keep up. At some point, either real wages catch up, the state redistributes more, debt fills the gap, or demand eventually slows.

The main question will be whether those productivity gains eventually spread to wages and purchasing power as well.

*BLS link: https://t.co/ljtDrVkdsD

A neat insight that I first heard from my good friend and legend @PermabullNino.

This chart shows Thermo-price (lowest red), which is the all-time-average production price for mined coins. 

Each cycle, the bear has bottomed multiples higher, representing a monetary premium.

The first 2011 cycle bottomed on the Thermo-price at a 1x multiple. Then 2015 based above a 2x. The 2018 and 2022 bears bottomed around a 6x or 7x premium.

This cycles bear bottomed at around a 12x and we're back to a 16x.

Thew other observation is that then area under the oscillator curve is getting larger, suggesting a more sustained monetary premium is developing over production cost with time.

Tops have approached the 32x multiple ($313k today), but if this trend of rising floors continues, eventually the floor meets the top...and then shit gets really weird!
